item.title: A browser tab
item.description:
The toolkit is pure Go with no DOM dependency, so GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm builds it like any other target. Two ways to put the result in front of somebody:

A plain canvas

go-widgets/webcanvas blits an RGBA framebuffer into a <canvas> and routes DOM pointer and keyboard events back into the scene. No compositor, no SharedArrayBuffer, no cross-origin isolation headers: any static host serves it.

//go:build js && wasm

package main

import "github.com/go-widgets/webcanvas"

func main() { webcanvas.Run("screen", myScene()) }

The scene implements App: Size, Draw(buf []byte), and one method per kind of event, each reporting whether anything changed so an unchanged frame is not repainted. It may also implement Ticker, Animator, Resizer,Scroller or ScrollConsumer.

Several canvases on one page

Run never returns and serves one canvas. webcanvas.Mount(canvas, scene) puts a scene on any <canvas> element, returns a *Surface at once, and can be called as often as the page needs (an editor in each cell of a notebook,say). Run is Mount, then Focus, then a park.

  • Keys go to the surface that has focus and to no other. The canvas getstabindex="0" unless the page set one, so a click or Tab focuses it, andSurface.Focus() does the same from code. (Before webcanvas v0.10.0 the key listeners were on window, and every canvas received every key.)
  • The wheel goes to the surface under the pointer. A scene that implementsScrollConsumer, Scroll(x, y, dx, dy int) (repaint, consumed bool),returns consumed == false when it did not use the event, and then the page scrolls under the canvas. A Scroller always takes the wheel, as before.
  • Surface.Close() removes every listener, timer and animation frame the surface installed.

The gallery andapp-template run this way.

Accessibility: the mirror

To a screen reader a <canvas> is one opaque image. A scene that also implements webcanvas.A11yAware, A11yNodes() []webcanvas.A11yNode, gets anaccessibility mirror (webcanvas v0.11.0): a DOM subtree beside the canvas that states in ARIA what the scene paints. A scene that does not implement it is unchanged.

func (s *scene) A11yNodes() []webcanvas.A11yNode {
 return []webcanvas.A11yNode{
 {Key: "Button#0", Role: "button", Name: "Save", X: 10, Y: 20, W: 80, H: 30},
 {Key: "@status", Role: "status", Name: s.message, X: 10, Y: 60, W: 200, H: 16},
 }
}
  • Nodes are listed in reading order, in surface pixels, with a Key that stays the same for the same widget from frame to frame (the toolkit’sA11yNode.Key). The mirror diffs by Key, so an unchanged widget keeps the same DOM element and a screen reader’s cursor is not reset on every frame.
  • Roles include button (a native <button>), checkbox, switch and radio,slider, progressbar, meter and spinbutton, text, textbox, status, alert and log. Any other WAI-ARIA role name is passed through.
  • Hidden from the eye, not from assistive technology. The mirror is clipped(clip-path: inset(50%)), never display: none, visibility: hidden oraria-hidden, which would remove it from the accessibility tree. It ignores the pointer, so the mouse still reaches the canvas.
  • Focus and keys. The element of the focused widget holds DOM focus, and keys are heard there.
  • Activation. A click on a mirror element, which is what a screen reader’s“activate” sends, is replayed as a press and release at the widget’s centre.
  • Announcements. Text that appears or changes in a status or log node is announced from one persistent polite live region, and alert text from an assertive one.
  • Cost. A changed tree reaches the DOM at most every 200 ms, and a change held back is applied later, never lost. An unchanged tree costs a signature.In headless Chrome, 2,000 nodes take about 70 ms to build and about 6 ms to update when one node changes (indicative, measured on a busy machine).
  • Untrusted text. Names and values are set only as text and attribute values, never as markup, so a notebook from anyone cannot inject HTML through a widget name.

Surface.Refresh() draws a frame and updates the mirror, for a host that changed the scene from outside. A text field is exposed as role=textbox with its text for now; an editing element for a focused field is planned.

Or let window choose. Since window v0.87.0,window.Open built for js/wasm on an ordinary page returns a back-end that draws into the page’s <canvas> (Config.Canvas, default "screen") through webcanvas. An application written against window then runs unchanged as a native window, in a browser tab, and in wasmdesk.

On the GPU

webcanvas.RunWith(id, app, presenter) takes a Presenter, and the packagewebcanvas/gpu provides one that draws frames with WebGPU.

  • How: an App that also implements Paint(painter.Painter) is recorded through gpupainter into ago-gfx/gpu2d list. Its WebGPU renderer draws the frame, which is copied into the canvas texture on the GPU.
  • Why a presenter: a canvas takes one context kind for life, so the presenter decides once, before the first frame.
  • Exactness: the pixels are the CPU Draw frame’s, byte for byte (a test holds it).
  • Fallbacks: a browser without WebGPU, or an App without Paint, stays on the 2D canvas. Neither is an error.

The web gallery draws this way.

A window on the wasmdesk desktop

Inside a wasmdesk worker, window.Open returns a client of the wasmdesk/wasmbox browser compositor. It allocates its surface in a SharedArrayBuffer, sayshello over its MessagePort, waits for welcome, paints into the shared buffer and posts commit — the whole surface, or only the damaged rectangles.The compositor’s input messages become toolkit.Event, as on X11.

So an application written against window runs unchanged as a native window and as a window of a desktop in a browser tab. Thedesktop shell demo does exactly that, from one source.

The protocol codec is covered at 100% on every platform. The live proof runs headless Chromium against the real wasmdesk compositor: it spawns the client,reads the compositor’s own composited pixels, clicks, and checks that the click reached the widget.
